Bundled optional component of minikube such as ingress, metrics-server, dashboard or registry, enabled with one command.
minikube command that gives LoadBalancer Services an external IP on your machine and forwards traffic to them.
Load balancer implementation for clusters without a cloud, assigning external IPs to LoadBalancer Services.
Kubernetes plugin interface that gives pods network connectivity (Calico, Cilium, Flannel, kindnet).
Tool that converts a Docker Compose file into Kubernetes manifests.
Development environment that runs in a container defined by devcontainer.json in the repository, giving every developer the same tools.
Small versioned installer, published as an OCI artifact, that adds a tool such as Java or the Docker CLI to a dev container.
GitHub's cloud development environments, which run dev containers on managed virtual machines.
Running a separate Docker daemon inside a container; isolated from the host's containers but needs privileged mode.
Mounting the host's Docker socket into a container so it uses the host daemon; simple, but equivalent to root access on the host.
Building a dev container image in CI ahead of time and publishing it, so developers open the project in seconds.
A service that keeps nothing between requests in its own memory or disk, so any instance can handle any request and instances can be added or replaced freely.
A service that holds data of its own between requests, such as a database or broker, so it needs stable identity, replication and careful recovery.
Load balancer setting that sends a client to the same instance every time so it can keep a session in memory; fragile, because the session is lost when that instance goes away.
A table or view shaped for a particular screen or query, built by projecting events or changes from the write side; eventually consistent.
Code that converts an old version of a stored event into the current shape when it is read, so event structures can change without rewriting history.
An immutable fact about something that happened in the business, named in the past tense, such as MoneyWithdrawn.
Append-only storage that keeps one ordered stream of events per aggregate and rejects concurrent appends with the same version.
The stream version a writer believes is current when it appends events; the store rejects the append if another writer got there first (optimistic concurrency).
A new event that corrects an earlier mistake, such as a reversal, because stored events are never edited or deleted.
A stable, deliberately designed event published for other services, kept separate from the detailed internal events of one aggregate.
Making personal data in an immutable log unreadable by deleting the encryption key that was used for that customer's data.
Java framework for event sourcing and CQRS with annotations for aggregates, command, event and query handlers, plus an event store (Axon Server) and Spring Boot support.
Event listener that turns events into a read model and records the last processed position so duplicates and restarts are safe.
The shared vocabulary that business experts and developers use, in conversation and in the code, within one bounded context.
A diagram of how bounded contexts relate: customer-supplier APIs, shared events, conformist, or an anti-corruption layer.
A translation layer that converts another system's model into your own, so its quirks and changes do not leak into your domain.
Workshop technique where domain experts and developers place business events on a wall to discover processes and bounded contexts.
A system split into services that are still tightly coupled (shared database, joint deploys, long sync chains), with the cost of microservices and none of the benefits.
Technique for replacing a component gradually: put an interface in front of it, then swap the implementation (for example for a remote call) behind that interface.
Observation that systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds them.
Reading a database's change log to publish every insert, update and delete as events, so other systems can stay in step without changing the application.
Refusing some requests early when a service is overloaded, ideally the least important, so the accepted ones stay fast.
Returning a reduced but useful result when a dependency fails, for example leaving out optional data or using a cached value.
Sending a second request to another instance when the first is slow and using whichever answers first, to cut tail latency; for idempotent reads only.
Planning timeouts so each inner call is shorter than the outer one and the whole chain fits in the time the user will wait.
RPC framework using Protobuf contracts over HTTP/2, with generated typed clients and servers, streaming and deadlines; common for internal service calls.
Compact binary serialisation format defined by .proto files, used by gRPC; field numbers must never be reused.
A gateway or BFF calling several services in parallel and merging the results into one response for the client.
Standard JSON format for HTTP API errors with type, title, status, detail and extra fields; supported in Spring as ProblemDetail.
Describes how the time or memory an algorithm needs grows with the input size n, ignoring constants and lower-order terms: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).
The average cost per operation over a sequence, when an occasional operation is expensive; for example ArrayList.add is O(1) amortised even though it sometimes copies the array.
Finds a value in sorted data by comparing with the middle element and discarding half the range each step, in O(log n) time.
Divide-and-conquer sort that splits the data in half, sorts each half and merges them; O(n log n) in every case, stable, needs O(n) extra memory.
Divide-and-conquer sort that partitions around a pivot so smaller elements go left and larger right, then sorts both sides; O(n log n) on average, O(n²) worst case, in place, not stable.
A sort that keeps equal elements in their original relative order, which matters when sorting by several keys one after another.
An algorithm that uses only O(1) or O(log n) extra memory instead of a copy of its input.
A queue that always returns the smallest element, or the one with the highest priority, first; in Java it is built on a binary heap with O(log n) add and remove.
Tree where each node is a character and each path spells a word, so all words with a given prefix are found in time proportional to the prefix length.
Graph representation that stores, for each node, the list of its neighbours; uses O(V + E) memory and suits sparse graphs.
Graph traversal that uses a queue and visits nodes level by level; finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph in O(V + E).
Graph traversal that uses a stack or recursion and follows one path as deep as possible before backing up; suits cycle detection and exploring all paths.
Shortest-path algorithm for graphs with non-negative weights that repeatedly takes the closest unfinished node from a priority queue.
Ordering of the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so that every node comes after the nodes it depends on.
Data structure that groups items into sets and answers whether two items are in the same set in near-constant time.
Technique that moves two indices through the data, often from both ends of sorted data, so one pass replaces nested loops.
Technique that keeps a moving range over an array or string and updates the answer as elements enter and leave, so the whole scan is O(n).
Array of running totals computed once, so the sum of any range is found in O(1) as a difference of two entries.
A stack kept in increasing or decreasing order, used to find the next greater or smaller element in O(n).
Solving a problem by storing the answers to smaller overlapping subproblems so each is computed once.
Caching the result of a function for each input so repeated calls return instantly; the top-down form of dynamic programming.
Exploring choices recursively: make a choice, recurse, then undo it and try the next, pruning choices that cannot lead to a solution.
Makes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders; correct only when that choice provably leads to a global optimum.
Splitting a problem into smaller parts, solving each part, and combining the results, as in merge sort and quicksort.
A last-in, first-out collection: push on top, pop from the top. Think of a pile of plates.
more: In Java use ArrayDeque (push, pop, peek) rather than the legacy Stack class.

short: The algorithm that finds unreachable objects and frees their memory: Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC or Shenandoah.
more: Each collector trades throughput, pause time and memory footprint differently. Not the same as the Stream Collector.

short: A named permission the client asks for, such as read:accounts. The token carries the scopes the user approved.
more: Scopes limit what an access token can do. They are not the same as a Spring bean scope.

short: A random value the client puts in the login request and checks inside the ID token, so a replayed or stolen token is rejected.
more: Different from the crypto nonce, which is a value used once per encryption.

short: A method name plus its parameter types. Java uses it to tell overloads apart; the return type and exceptions are not part of it.
Automating where containers run, restarting them when they fail, scaling them and letting them find each other.
more: Kubernetes is the standard orchestrator. Do not confuse it with saga orchestration.

short: A named minikube cluster (minikube -p name). Each profile has its own node and kubectl context.
A machine (in kind, a container) that runs pods. The control plane decides which node each pod goes to.
Keeps only the elements that match a Predicate and drops the rest. It is lazy and runs when a terminal operation starts.
A read model built by replaying events and updating a query-friendly view as new events arrive.
more: Projections can be thrown away and rebuilt from the event log.

short: Rearranging a range around a pivot so smaller values sit on the left and larger on the right, then returning the pivot index.
A one-way function that turns any input into a fixed-size digest (SHA-256). The same input gives the same digest; you cannot go back.
more: Used for integrity checks, signatures and password storage (with a salt and a slow algorithm).

short: Rows and columns of one kind of record in a relational database, such as accounts or transfers.
A Java build tool: a pom.xml describes the project, a fixed lifecycle orders the steps, and plugin goals do the work.
more: Dependencies come from repositories by group, artifact and version.

short: A build tool that models a build as a graph of tasks with declared inputs and outputs, so it can skip, cache and parallelise work.
more: Build files are Kotlin or Groovy code.

short: The Maven file that describes a project: its coordinates, dependencies, plugins and parent.
more: mvn help:effective-pom shows the result after inheritance and defaults.

short: groupId, artifactId and version: the three values that identify an artifact in a repository.
more: A classifier or packaging type can be added.

short: The fixed, ordered list of Maven phases (compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy). Running a phase runs all earlier ones.
A task provided by a Maven plugin, such as compiler:compile. Goals are bound to lifecycle phases or run directly.
Maven plugins that run tests: Surefire runs unit tests in the test phase, Failsafe runs integration tests and checks them in verify.
The folder ~/.m2/repository where Maven caches downloaded artifacts and stores what you install.
The main public repository of Java libraries, where Maven and Gradle download dependencies from by default.
A server that proxies Maven Central and hosts a company's private artifacts, so builds are faster and controlled.
The per-user Maven file in ~/.m2 for mirrors, repository credentials, proxies and profiles that must not be committed.
Maven's conflict rule: the version closest to your project in the dependency tree is used, and the first declared wins a tie. It is not the newest version.
A pom section that fixes the version and scope of artifacts without adding them, so children and transitive dependencies use one version.
A pom or platform that only lists compatible library versions, such as spring-boot-dependencies. You import it and then omit versions.
Says where a Maven dependency is on the classpath: compile, provided, runtime, test or import.
Removes one unwanted transitive dependency from a single dependency in Maven or Gradle.
The part of Maven that sorts the modules of a multi-module build by their dependencies and builds them in that order.
One build made of several modules, each with its own build file, usually sharing a parent and building in dependency order.
A named set of changes to a Maven build, activated with -P or by a property, JDK or operating system.
A small script committed with the project (mvnw or gradlew) that downloads the exact Maven or Gradle version, so everyone and CI build with the same one.
A version ending in -SNAPSHOT: work in progress that can change and is re-checked for updates. Release versions never change.
Gradle's directed acyclic graph of tasks, built in the configuration phase from their dependencies. Only needed tasks run.
A unit of work in Gradle with actions, dependencies and declared inputs and outputs, such as compileJava or test.
Gradle skips a task whose inputs and outputs match its last run. FROM-CACHE means the outputs came from the build cache.
Gradle stores task outputs by input hash, locally or on a shared server, and reuses them across branches, machines and CI.
Saves Gradle's task graph so a repeated build can skip the configuration phase.
A background JVM that stays warm between Gradle builds, so there is no JVM start-up and build logic stays compiled.
A named group of Gradle dependencies with a purpose. implementation is internal, api is exposed to consumers, runtimeOnly is run time only.
A gradle/libs.versions.toml file listing library versions and plugins once, used from every project by name such as libs.jackson.databind.
A small Gradle plugin that holds shared build configuration, applied by each project instead of copying settings.
A setting that tells the build which JDK version to compile and test with (Gradle toolchains, Maven toolchains plugin), whichever JDK runs the build tool itself.
A file listing every object on the Java heap and the references between them. Used to find what holds memory in a leak.
more: Take one with jcmd GC.heap_dump or -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError. It contains sensitive data, so protect it.

short: The JDK command that sends diagnostic commands to a running JVM by process id: Thread.print, GC.heap_dump, VM.native_memory, JFR.start and more.
The memory that would be freed if an object disappeared: the object plus everything only it keeps alive.
The memory taken by an object itself, without the objects it refers to.
Eclipse Memory Analyzer: a tool that opens heap dumps and shows leak suspects, the dominator tree and the path to GC roots.
A profile drawn as stacked boxes: each box is a method, its width is the share of samples where it was on the stack. Left-to-right order has no meaning.
A tool that shows where a program spends its time or memory, by sampling stacks or recording events. Java Flight Recorder and async-profiler are examples.
A low-overhead sampling profiler for the JVM that produces flame graphs without waiting for safepoints.
A JVM feature (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking) that reports memory use outside the heap by area: threads, classes, code, GC, internal. Read it with jcmd VM.native_memory.
HotSpot first interprets bytecode, then compiles hot methods with C1 and, if they stay hot, with the more optimising C2.
The memory area where the JIT stores compiled machine code. If it fills up, compilation stops and the program slows down.
The JVM discarding optimised code whose assumptions no longer hold, and falling back to slower code until it recompiles.
A checked exception thrown when code loads a class by name at run time and the class loader cannot find it.
An error thrown when a class that existed at compile time is missing or failed to initialise at run time. Often a missing transitive dependency.
A count of instances and bytes per class on the heap (jcmd GC.class_histogram). A quick leak hint without a full heap dump.
The ability of a program to inspect and use classes, fields, methods and constructors at run time, by name, through java.lang.reflect.
more: Frameworks use it to create beans, call setters and read annotations. It is slower than a direct call and loses compile-time checks.

short: The single method invoke(proxy, method, args) that receives every call made on a JDK dynamic proxy. It runs your extra code and may call the real object.
A typed, directly executable reference to a method or field. Faster than reflection when stored in a static final field. Lambdas are built on them.
An annotation placed on another annotation, such as @Retention, @Target or @Inherited. Spring also uses the word for composed annotations like @RestController.
How long an annotation is kept: SOURCE (compiler only), CLASS (class file, the default) or RUNTIME (readable by reflection).
A plug-in that runs inside the compiler, reads annotated source and generates new classes. MapStruct and Dagger work this way. No run-time cost.
A compile-time tool that adds getters, builders and constructors to the compiler's syntax tree from annotations such as @Getter and @Builder.
An annotation processor that generates mapper classes to copy data between objects such as entities and DTOs, with no reflection at run time.
A library that generates and changes classes at run time. Hibernate uses it for lazy proxies and Mockito for mocks.
A small library that creates an object without calling its constructor. Spring uses it so a CGLIB proxy can be built for a class whose constructor needs arguments.
The exception that Method.invoke uses to wrap an exception thrown by the called method. Call getCause() to get the real one.
The most widely used Java JSON library. It reads and writes objects through reflection (getters, setters, fields, annotations such as @JsonProperty).
The standard Java unit testing framework. JUnit 5 finds methods annotated @Test by reflection and runs them.
An Exception that is not a RuntimeException (IOException, SQLException). The compiler forces the caller to catch it or declare it with throws.
A RuntimeException or an Error. The compiler does not force you to handle it. Usually a bug or a broken rule, such as a null or a bad argument.
A second exception, thrown while cleaning up (for example by close()), attached to the primary one with addSuppressed instead of replacing it.
more: try-with-resources does this automatically. Read them with getSuppressed().

short: Passing the original exception as the cause of a new one, so the stack trace shows "Caused by:" and the root cause is not lost.
Catching a low-level exception and throwing one that belongs to the current layer, with the original as the cause. Spring turns SQLException into DataAccessException this way.
The list of method calls active when an exception was created, innermost first. Read the top line and then the "Caused by:" lines.
The Throwable method that records the call stack when an exception is created. It is the main cost of an exception and can be disabled with the 4-argument constructor.
The interface (one method, close()) that a resource implements so it can be declared in a try-with-resources header and closed automatically.
catch (A | B e): one block for several unrelated exception types. The variable is implicitly final.
A JDK RuntimeException that wraps an IOException, used to throw an I/O failure from a lambda or a stream where checked exceptions are not allowed.
The root class of everything that can be thrown. Its two subclasses are Error and Exception. It holds the message, the cause, the stack trace and the suppressed exceptions.
Continuous integration and continuous delivery (or deployment): an automatic path that builds, tests and releases every change.
Merging small changes into the main branch often, with every merge built and tested automatically, so integration problems show up within minutes.
Every change that passes the pipeline is ready to release through an automated path, and a person decides when to go live.
Every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically, with no human approval step.
The automated sequence of steps (build, test, scan, package, deploy) that every change goes through on the way to production.
The deployable output of a build, such as a JAR or a container image. Built once, versioned, and promoted unchanged through the environments.
An automatic rule in the pipeline (tests pass, coverage, no critical vulnerability) that stops the change if it fails.
Everyone integrates into main, or into branches that live hours, and hides unfinished work behind feature flags.
A configuration switch that turns code on or off at run time. It separates deploying code from releasing a feature.
A branching model with long-lived develop, release and hotfix branches. Suits versioned products but delays integration.
A request to merge a branch into another, where a reviewer reads the change and the pipeline runs its checks before the merge.
Four delivery measures: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore. Two for speed, two for stability.
A quick check after a deployment that the new version starts and answers its most basic calls.
Restoring the previous version of an application after a bad release, usually by redeploying the previous artifact.
A widely used open-source automation server. Pipelines are written in a Jenkinsfile, in declarative or scripted Groovy syntax.
The CI/CD service built into GitHub. Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows, run on events such as a push or a pull request.
A static analysis server that reports bugs, vulnerabilities, code smells, duplication and coverage, and applies a quality gate to new code.
Software bill of materials: a list of every component and version inside an application, used to find affected systems when a vulnerability is announced.
A set of rules for cloud-ready services. Factor III keeps configuration in the environment, outside the build artifact.
A GitHub service that opens pull requests to update dependencies and fix known vulnerabilities.
An open-source scanner for vulnerabilities in container images, dependencies, configuration files and secrets.
A way to change a database without downtime: add the new structure, move the code and data over, and only later remove the old structure.
The plan for replacing the running version with a new one: recreate, rolling update, blue-green, canary and so on.
Copies of real requests sent to a new version whose responses are discarded, to test it under real load with no user impact. It must have no side effects.
Running new code in production without showing its result to users, only logging or comparing it.
Showing version A to some users and B to others to compare a business metric such as conversion. A product experiment, not a safety mechanism.
In a Kubernetes rolling update, how many pods above the desired count may exist at the same time (extra capacity).
In a Kubernetes rolling update, how many pods may be missing at the same time. 0 means capacity never drops.
A Kubernetes controller for progressive delivery: canary and blue-green releases with traffic weights and automatic metric analysis.
A progressive delivery operator that automates canary and blue-green releases using a service mesh or ingress and metrics.
Releasing a new version gradually (canary, blue-green, flags) and deciding each step from real metrics, with automatic rollback.
How many users or systems a failure affects. Canary releases and feature flags keep it small.
On a stop signal, the application stops taking new requests, finishes the current ones and then exits. In Spring Boot: server.shutdown=graceful.
A feature flag that turns a risky feature off at once, without a deployment.
Filling a new column or table with data computed from existing rows, usually in small batches so it does not lock the table.
A popular service mesh for Kubernetes. It splits traffic by weight, retries, times out and secures calls between services with sidecar proxies.
Infrastructure as a service: you rent virtual machines, storage and networks and manage the OS and everything above. Example: EC2.
Platform as a service: you deploy code and the provider manages the OS, runtime, patching and scaling. Example: Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service.
Software as a service: a finished application run by the provider. You only use and configure it. Example: Microsoft 365.
Running code without managing servers. A function runs on an event, scales to zero when idle, and is billed per call.
A geographic area of a cloud provider with several availability zones, for example Singapore (ap-southeast-1). Data stays in the region you choose.
One or more separate data centres inside a region with independent power, cooling and network. Zones fail independently.
Running a service, or a database with a synchronous standby, in more than one availability zone so a zone failure does not stop it.
Keeping a system working through the failure of a component, by removing single points of failure and spreading over zones.
Restoring a service after a large failure such as the loss of a region. Planned with an RTO and an RPO.
Recovery time objective: the longest time a service may be down after a failure.
Recovery point objective: the most data a failure may lose, measured in time (for example the last 5 minutes).
The ability to add and remove capacity automatically as the load changes, so you do not pay for idle resources.
A cloud feature that adds or removes instances by a policy, such as keeping average CPU at 60 percent, within a minimum and a maximum.
The provider secures the cloud (hardware, facilities, hypervisor). The customer secures what is in it: identities, data, configuration, guest OS.
Identity and access management: users, roles and policies that say who may do which action on which resource. The default is deny.
Giving an identity only the permissions it needs, on only the resources it needs, for as long as it needs them.
Your private network inside a cloud region, divided into public and private subnets, with security groups acting as firewalls.
A stateful virtual firewall attached to an instance or interface that allows listed traffic and denies the rest.
Elastic Compute Cloud: AWS virtual machines (IaaS).
Simple Storage Service: AWS object storage for files, backups and data lakes, with very high durability. Buckets are private by default.
Elastic Kubernetes Service: AWS managed Kubernetes control plane. Azure has AKS and Google Cloud has GKE.
A network of edge locations that cache content close to users to cut latency and absorb load. Example: CloudFront.
Spare cloud capacity sold at a large discount that the provider can reclaim at short notice. Good for batch and stateless work.
The practice of managing cloud cost: tagging, budgets, right-sizing, commitments and shared ownership by engineering and finance.
The cost and effort of leaving a provider because of proprietary services. Managed services bring some of it, so decide where it is acceptable.
The rule or choice that data stays in a given country or region. In the cloud it is controlled by the region you pick.
On-premises systems and public cloud used together over a private link such as Direct Connect or ExpressRoute.
Designed for the cloud: small stateless services, config in the environment, automation, infrastructure as code, observability.
Moving an application to cloud virtual machines with little change. Quick, but gets few of the cloud benefits.
A secure, multi-account cloud base with networking, identity, logging and guardrails, built before applications move in.
A text file in the repository that defines a Jenkins pipeline as code, in declarative (pipeline { }) or scripted (node { }) Groovy.
The central Jenkins server: UI, job configuration, build queue and history. It schedules work and should not run builds itself.
A machine, container or pod that connects to the Jenkins controller and runs the build steps. Selected by labels.
A slot on a Jenkins agent that runs one build at a time.
The structured Jenkinsfile syntax: pipeline { agent, stages, steps, post }. Validated before it runs, and the recommended default.
The free-form Groovy Jenkinsfile syntax, starting with node { }. More powerful and easier to make unreadable.
A Jenkins job that creates a pipeline for every branch and pull request that has a Jenkinsfile, and removes it when the branch is deleted.
A Git repository of Groovy code that Jenkinsfiles import with @Library, so common pipeline steps are written once. Pin its version.
Jenkins Configuration as Code: the controller settings in a YAML file in Git, so a controller can be recreated and changes reviewed.
The CI/CD system built into GitLab. The pipeline is defined in .gitlab-ci.yml and executed by runners.
A separate program that polls GitLab for jobs and runs them with an executor such as Docker or Kubernetes. Shared, group or project scope.
The file in a repository that declares GitLab pipeline stages, jobs, scripts, rules and artifacts.
Files such as dependencies stored between pipelines to speed jobs up. Best effort: a job must still work when the cache is empty.
A tool that builds container images inside a container or pod without a Docker daemon or privileged mode. Common in GitLab and Jenkins on Kubernetes.
A pipeline where jobs declare needs: and start as soon as the jobs they depend on finish, without waiting for the whole stage.
A GitLab pipeline that runs for a merge request. It builds and tests the change and normally does not deploy.
A GitLab CI variable passed only to pipelines on protected branches and tags, so feature branches cannot read production secrets.
A GitLab environment where only named roles may deploy, with optional required approvals. Gives four-eyes control on production.
A Jenkins pipeline step that makes an older build abort if a newer build has already passed that point, so an old deploy cannot overwrite a new one.
Amazon Web Services: the largest public cloud, with more than two hundred services in regions and availability zones worldwide.
Elastic Container Service: the AWS container orchestrator. Runs tasks and services on EC2 or on Fargate.
Serverless compute for ECS and EKS containers: you define CPU and memory, AWS runs the container with no nodes to manage.
Relational Database Service: managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server and MariaDB with backups, patching and multi-AZ failover.
AWS cloud-built relational database, MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible, with fast failover, shared storage and up to 15 read replicas.
AWS serverless key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale. Needs known access patterns, no joins.
Managed Redis and Memcached on AWS, used for caching, sessions and rate limits.
The AWS content delivery network. Caches content at edge locations and fronts S3 or an application, with TLS and WAF.
AWS DNS service with health checks and routing policies such as failover, latency and weighted.
Application Load Balancer: a layer 7 AWS load balancer with path and host routing. NLB is the layer 4 one.
Simple Queue Service: AWS managed message queue. At-least-once delivery, visibility timeout, dead-letter queues, FIFO option.
Simple Notification Service: AWS publish and subscribe topics that push a message to many subscribers such as SQS queues and Lambda.
AWS event bus that routes events from AWS services, your apps and SaaS partners to targets by rules, and runs schedules.
AWS service for ordered, replayable data streams. MSK is the managed Kafka alternative.
Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka: AWS managed Kafka clusters.
AWS managed workflow service that coordinates steps as a state machine, with retries, error handling and parallel branches.
AWS infrastructure as code. Templates in YAML or JSON describe resources, and a stack creates and updates them. CDK generates them from code.
AWS Cloud Development Kit: define infrastructure in Java, TypeScript or Python, which synthesises to CloudFormation.
AWS monitoring service for metrics, logs, alarms and dashboards.
AWS service that records every API call in an account (who, what, when, from where). The base of the audit trail.
AWS service that stores secrets and rotates them automatically. Parameter Store is the cheaper option for plain configuration.
AWS sign-up and sign-in service for the users of your own applications, supporting OAuth 2.0, OIDC and social login.
Web application firewall: filters HTTP requests by rules (SQL injection, rate limits, bad IPs) in front of CloudFront, ALB or API Gateway.
AWS threat detection service that analyses logs and network activity for suspicious behaviour.
Service that groups many AWS accounts into organisational units with consolidated billing and service control policies.
A guardrail in AWS Organizations that sets the maximum permissions in an account or OU. It limits and never grants.
AWS service that builds a governed multi-account landing zone with baseline controls and logging.
AWS single sign-on to many accounts using the company identity provider, with permission sets per account.
A managed AWS service that lets resources in private subnets reach the internet without being reachable from it. Billed per hour and per GB.
A private connection from a VPC to an AWS service such as S3, so traffic does not use the public internet.
IAM roles for service accounts: lets a Kubernetes pod on EKS assume an AWS role with temporary credentials.
Archive storage classes of S3 for rarely read data, cheap to store, with retrieval times from minutes to hours.
A commitment to a steady amount of AWS usage for one or three years in return for a large discount on the on-demand price.
A dedicated private network link between a company data centre and AWS, with steady latency and no public internet.
An AWS hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks, instead of a mesh of peering links.
Spring integration for AWS: @SqsListener, SqsTemplate, S3 resources, Secrets Manager and Parameter Store as property sources.
Amazon Machine Image: the image an EC2 instance starts from, holding the OS and software. A golden AMI is built and patched by a pipeline.
A versioned definition of how to launch an EC2 instance (AMI, type, role, security groups, user data). Auto Scaling groups use it.
A managed fleet of EC2 instances from a launch template, with a minimum, desired and maximum size across zones, replacing unhealthy ones and scaling by policy.
An Auto Scaling policy that works like a thermostat: it adds or removes capacity to keep a metric, such as average CPU, near a target.
An Auto Scaling feature that replaces instances in batches with a new launch template version, as a rolling deployment with automatic rollback.
The session-based version of the EC2 instance metadata service. Requiring it blocks SSRF attacks that steal the instance role credentials.
AWS ARM-based processors (instance types with a g, such as m7g). Usually about 20 percent cheaper for similar performance.
The extra time of the first call to a new Lambda environment: download the code, start the runtime, run init. Large for Java frameworks.
A Lambda feature that restores a function from a snapshot of its initialised environment, cutting Java cold starts. Refresh unique state after restore.
A Lambda setting that keeps a number of execution environments initialised and ready, so calls do not hit a cold start. Costs extra.
A Lambda setting that caps and guarantees the concurrent executions of one function. It also protects the database behind it.
A Lambda SQS feature: the handler returns the ids of the failed messages, and only those return to the queue instead of the whole batch.
The ECS blueprint of a task: container images, CPU, memory, ports, secrets, logging, health check and the task and execution roles.
An ECS object that keeps a desired number of tasks running, replaces failed ones, registers them with a load balancer and handles deployments.
In ECS, the task role is what the application uses to call AWS. The execution role is what ECS uses to pull the image, read secrets and write logs.
An EKS feature, like IRSA, that lets a pod assume a specific IAM role with temporary credentials.
A Kubernetes node provisioner for EKS that launches the best-fitting instance for pending pods, including Spot, and consolidates underused nodes.
An AWS service that runs a web app or container from source or an image, with automatic scaling and almost no configuration.
An AWS service that runs queued batch jobs on managed compute, often on Spot.
A managed connection pool for RDS and Aurora. Stops many Lambda functions from exhausting database connections.
Storage of whole objects addressed by a key through an API, with no file system. Example: S3. Scales without limit and is shared by any client.
A raw disk attached to one server, which formats it and can change any block. Example: EBS. Low latency, one instance at a time.
A shared file system with directories that many servers mount at once. Example: EFS over NFS, FSx.
An S3 option that trades access speed and retrieval cost for price: Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, the Glacier tiers.
An S3 rule that moves objects to cheaper classes or deletes them by age, and removes old versions and unfinished multipart uploads.
A time-limited URL signed with credentials that allows one operation on one S3 object, so a client can upload or download directly.
Uploading a large S3 object in parts, in parallel and restartable. Recommended above about 100 MB.
S3 keeps every version of an object. A delete adds a delete marker, so earlier data can be restored.
S3 write once, read many protection. Governance mode can be bypassed by privileged users, compliance mode cannot until retention ends.
Write once, read many: data that cannot be changed or deleted during its retention period. Required for some financial records.
S3 setting, on the account or bucket, that stops any bucket policy or ACL from making data public. The most important S3 control.
S3 server-side encryption with a KMS key you control and audit. SSE-S3 uses keys that S3 manages.
S3 copies new objects asynchronously to a bucket in another region, for disaster recovery or latency. Needs versioning.
An incremental point-in-time backup of an EBS volume, stored in S3. Can restore to any zone and be copied across regions and accounts.
A fast local disk on the EC2 host. Its data disappears when the instance stops or fails. For caches and scratch space only.
Elastic File System: managed NFS shared by many instances and containers across zones. Grows and shrinks by itself.
A service that applies one backup plan to many AWS services, copies to other regions and accounts, and can lock the vault.
AWS Backup feature that makes a vault immutable: recovery points cannot be deleted before their retention ends, even by administrators.
The cheapest S3 class, for long-term retention of data read very rarely. Retrieval takes up to about 12 hours.
AWS managed SFTP, FTPS and FTP into S3 or EFS, used when partners exchange files with a bank.
An AWS service that copies large datasets between on-premises storage and AWS over the network, with scheduling and verification.
AWS managed relational database service. Runs PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server or Db2 and handles patching, backups and failover.
An asynchronous copy of a database that serves reads. It lags the primary, can be in another region and can be promoted.
Restoring a database to any second within the backup retention period (up to 35 days on RDS) into a new instance or table.
AWS cloud-built MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible database with shared storage across three zones, up to 15 readers and fast failover.
Aurora capacity that scales in small steps (ACUs) with the load, so a cluster follows spiky demand and can scale down to a minimum.
Aurora storage replicated to other regions in under a second, with local reads and a managed cross-region failover in about a minute.
AWS serverless key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond reads and writes at any scale. Designed around access patterns.
The optional DynamoDB key that orders items sharing a partition key, which allows range queries.
A DynamoDB index with its own partition and sort key, spanning the whole table. Eventually consistent and has its own capacity.
An ordered 24-hour log of item changes in a DynamoDB table, consumed by Lambda or Kinesis for projections and event publishing.
Multi-region, active-active DynamoDB replication with last-writer-wins conflict resolution.
An in-memory cache in front of DynamoDB that serves hot reads in microseconds.
A DynamoDB write that succeeds only if a condition holds, such as attribute_not_exists. Gives idempotency and optimistic locking.
AWS managed in-memory store (Redis OSS, Valkey, Memcached) used for caching, sessions and counters.
A Redis-compatible in-memory database that is durable through a multi-AZ transaction log, so it can be a primary database.
AWS service that migrates databases with a full load plus change data capture, so the source stays live until cut-over.
An RDS feature that keeps a synchronised copy of a database for a major upgrade or schema change, then switches over in about a minute.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing: an address range written as 10.0.0.0/16. Ranges of VPCs and data centres must not overlap if they will be connected.
A subnet whose route table has a route to an internet gateway. Holds only load balancers and NAT gateways.
A subnet with no route from the internet. Holds applications and databases, and reaches out through NAT or endpoints.
A list of destination ranges and targets that decides where a subnet sends its traffic. The 0.0.0.0/0 route to an internet gateway makes a subnet public.
The VPC component that connects it to the internet for resources with public addresses. No charge by itself.
A stateless subnet-level firewall with allow and deny rules in numbered order. A coarse extra layer next to security groups.
Private access to a service in another VPC or account through a network interface in your subnet. Only that service is reachable.
AWS layer 7 load balancer that routes HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC and WebSocket by host, path or header, with WAF and authentication support.
AWS layer 4 load balancer for TCP, UDP and TLS with a static IP per zone, very high throughput and low latency.
The set of targets behind a load balancer listener, with a health check. Only healthy targets receive traffic.
The time a load balancer lets in-flight requests finish when a target is removed. 300 seconds by default.
AWS DNS service with alias records, routing policies (weighted, latency, failover), health checks and private hosted zones.
A Route 53 record that points a name, including the bare domain, at an AWS resource, free of query charges and following its address changes.
AWS content delivery network with edge locations that cache content, end TLS and attach WAF close to users.
Managed API front door with authorizers, throttling, usage plans and integrations. Limits: about 29 seconds and 10 MB. Priced per request.
An API Gateway connection to resources in a VPC, such as an internal load balancer, so back ends need no public address.
An API Gateway REST API setting that limits how fast and how much each API key holder may call.
A dedicated private line from a data centre to AWS with steady latency and bandwidth. Use two for resilience.
Encrypted IPsec tunnels over the internet between a data centre and a VPC. Quick to set up, often the backup for Direct Connect.
A regional hub that connects many VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect with route tables, instead of a mesh of peerings.
A one-to-one private connection between two VPCs. Simple, but not transitive and needs non-overlapping ranges.
Records of the IP traffic accepted or rejected in a VPC, sent to S3 or CloudWatch for audit and troubleshooting.
Two static anycast IP addresses that route traffic over the AWS backbone to the closest healthy region, with fast failover without DNS caching.
Issues and automatically renews free TLS certificates for CloudFront, load balancers and API Gateway.
An AWS identity with permissions but no password or keys. A principal assumes it through STS and gets temporary credentials.
The service that issues temporary credentials when a role is assumed, valid from 15 minutes to 12 hours.
The policy on an IAM role that says who may assume it. The permissions policies say what the role may do.
A JSON document of statements with effect, action, resource and optional conditions. Everything is denied by default and an explicit deny wins.
An IAM limit on the most that an identity policy can grant a role or user. Used when teams may create their own roles.
Finds resources shared outside the account or organization and unused access, and generates policies from CloudTrail activity.
Creates and controls encryption keys. Key material never leaves KMS, every use is authorised by policy and logged in CloudTrail.
A KMS key whose policy, rotation and lifecycle you control. Banks use them for data in scope for the audit trail and control.
A key used to encrypt data itself, returned by KMS as a plaintext copy and a copy encrypted under the KMS key.
The resource policy on a KMS key. It is the root of access, and separates key administrators from key users.
Extra key-value data bound to a KMS ciphertext and logged. Decryption fails unless the same context is supplied.
A dedicated hardware security module under your sole control, for strict regulatory needs. Costlier than KMS.
Stores secrets encrypted with KMS, controls access, versions them and rotates them automatically through a Lambda function.
Systems Manager store for configuration values, plain or KMS-encrypted SecureString. Cheaper than Secrets Manager, no built-in rotation.
Sign-in service for application users: a user pool issues OIDC tokens, an identity pool exchanges tokens for AWS credentials.
Records every AWS API call (who, when, from where, what). Send an organization trail to a locked log account with validation.
Records resource configuration over time and checks it against rules, with conformance packs and automatic remediation.
Threat detection from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs: compromised credentials, crypto-mining, unusual API use.
Collects findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Config and partners across accounts, and scores them against standards like CIS and PCI DSS.
Scans EC2 instances, ECR images and Lambda functions for known vulnerabilities.
Finds sensitive data such as card numbers and personal data in S3 buckets.
Portal with AWS compliance reports and agreements, used as evidence in audits.
A tightly controlled, monitored emergency account or role used when normal sign-in is unavailable. Alarmed whenever it is used.
Lets servers outside AWS get temporary role credentials using an X.509 certificate from the bank own certificate authority.
A function together with the scope it was created in. It keeps reading and changing those variables after the outer function has returned.
Scope decided by where code is written: a function sees the variables of the scopes around it, innermost first (the scope chain).
Declarations are processed before the code runs. Functions are hoisted with their body, var as undefined, let and const stay in the temporal dead zone.
The span from the start of a block to the declaration of a let, const or class, where using the name throws a ReferenceError.
JavaScript mode that turns silent mistakes into errors and makes this undefined in a plain function call. On in ES modules and classes.
Short function syntax with no own this, arguments or prototype, so it uses the this of the enclosing scope. Not for object methods or constructors.
The object that another object inherits from. A property not found on the object is looked up on its prototype, then on that one, up to null.
Immediately invoked function expression: a function that is defined and called at once to create a private scope.
Syntax that pulls values out of an object by name or an array by position into variables, with defaults and rest: const { id, owner: { name } } = account.
The ... syntax that expands an array, object or iterable in place. Makes shallow copies and merges. The same symbol collects the rest in parameters.
The ?. operator reads a path or calls a function and returns undefined instead of throwing when something on the way is null or undefined.
The ?? operator returns its right side only when the left is null or undefined. Unlike ||, it keeps 0 and the empty string.
A value that counts as true in a condition. Everything except the falsy values, including "0", an empty array and an empty object.
Automatic conversion of a value to another type, for example by == or +. "5" + 3 is "53" but "5" - 3 is 2.
JavaScript integer type of any size, written 123n. Used beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, which is 2^53 - 1.
A copy of only the top-level object. Nested objects stay shared with the original. Made by spread, Object.assign or slice.
A copy where nothing is shared with the original, including nested objects. Made by structuredClone.
A function that takes functions as arguments or returns one, such as map, filter, setTimeout or a debounce wrapper.
The standard import and export module system. Static, so bundlers can tree-shake, always strict, with live bindings.
The older Node.js module system with require and module.exports. Loads synchronously at run time.
A bundler removing exports that are never imported, possible because ES module imports are static.
Wrapper that runs a function only after calls have stopped for a set time. Used for search-as-you-type.
Wrapper that lets a function run at most once per interval. Used for scroll and resize handlers.
A map whose keys are objects held weakly, so an entry does not stop its key from being garbage collected. Good for caches keyed by objects.
A function* that can pause at yield and resume, producing values lazily. Works with for...of.
A callback that keeps using old values of variables from the run where it was created, common in timers and React effects.
Runs when the call stack is empty: all microtasks first, then one task from the task queue, then repeats. Lets one thread handle many waiting operations.
The functions currently running. One runs to completion before anything else starts, so a long function blocks the whole page or server.
Queue of finished callbacks (timers, events, I/O) that the event loop takes one at a time, after the microtasks.
A promise callback, an await continuation or a queueMicrotask call. The event loop runs all microtasks before the next task.
An object for a value that arrives later. Pending, then settled once as fulfilled or rejected. then, catch and finally return new promises.
A function declared with async. It always returns a promise, and await pauses it without blocking the thread.
Deeply nested callbacks with repeated error handling, which promises and async/await replace.
Waits for all promises and fulfills with their values in order, or rejects with the first failure. Does not cancel the others.
A rejected promise with no handler. Logs an error in the browser and ends the Node.js process since version 15.
Creates an AbortSignal that cancels fetch and other APIs. AbortSignal.timeout makes a signal that aborts after a delay.
A script run on another browser thread with its own event loop, talking to the main thread by postMessage. For CPU-heavy work.
The C library behind the Node.js event loop and its thread pool (4 threads by default) for file system, DNS and crypto calls.
A Node.js callback queue that runs before promise microtasks, right after the current operation.
Schedules a callback as a task after at least the given delay. With 0 it still runs after all synchronous code and microtasks.
JavaScript with a static type system. The compiler checks types and then erases them, so nothing is checked at run time.
Type parameters such as first<T>(items: T[]): T that keep the link between input and output types. Support constraints (T extends X) and inference.
A TypeScript enum generates run-time code and numeric enums accept any number. A union of string literals or an as const object is usually better.
Types are compatible when their shapes fit, whatever their names. Java types are nominal and need an explicit implements.
The type-safe top type: any value can be assigned to it, but it must be narrowed before use. Use it instead of any for parsed JSON and caught errors.
The type with no values: a function that never returns, or what is left after every union member is handled. Used for exhaustive checks.
A value that is one of several types, written A | B. Only what all members share may be used until the value is narrowed.
A value that has all members of several types, written A & B. Used to combine object types.
A union whose members share a literal field, such as status. Checking that field narrows the whole object to one member.
The compiler refining a type inside a branch, after typeof, instanceof, in, equality checks, a discriminant or a type guard.
A function returning x is T that tells the compiler the type of a value when it returns true. Used to check unknown data.
value as T tells the compiler to trust you. Nothing is checked or converted at run time, so a wrong assertion fails later.
A type that is one exact value, such as "ok", 404 or true. A union of literals limits a value to a set and gives autocomplete.
Freezes a literal to its narrowest type, for example a readonly tuple of exact strings, so a union can be derived from it.
Checks a value against a type without widening it, so the exact literal types are kept.
Built-in types that build new types from old ones: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited.
A type built by iterating over the keys of another type, for example { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }. How Partial works.
A type chosen by a test, such as T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never. Distributes over unions.
Type operator that gives the union of the keys of a type. With T[K] (indexed access) it types property lookups.
The tsconfig strict option under which null and undefined are separate types that must be handled before use.
The TypeScript compiler configuration: target, module, strict options, jsx, include. Bundlers read it for type checking only.
A .d.ts file that describes the types of JavaScript code. Libraries ship them, or install @types packages.
A schema library that validates data at run time and derives the TypeScript type from the same schema.
A JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components. Declarative: you describe the UI for the current state and React updates the DOM.
Markup syntax inside JavaScript that a compiler turns into function calls creating element objects. Not HTML, not a string.
A function that takes props and returns JSX. Pure with respect to its props and state. The unit of reuse. Names start with a capital letter.
The read-only inputs a parent passes to a component, including children and callback functions.
Data a component remembers between renders. Changing it with the setter triggers a new render. A snapshot per render, updated with new values, never mutated.
A lightweight in-memory description of the UI. React compares the new one with the previous one and applies only the differences to the real DOM.
React comparing the new element tree with the previous one: same type and position updates, different type remounts, lists are matched by key.
React calling the component functions to compute the new element tree. Must be pure, and can be paused, repeated or thrown away.
A stable value, unique among siblings, that identifies a list item between renders. Use an id, not the index. Changing it resets the component state.
A form field whose value comes from React state and is updated in onChange, so the state is the single source of truth.
Moving state to the closest common parent of the components that need it and passing it down as props with callbacks to change it.
A function such as useState or useEffect that lets a function component use React features. Called only at the top level, in the same order every render.
A hook returning a mutable box { current } that survives renders and does not trigger a render. Used for DOM nodes and instance values.
The content between a component tags, passed as props.children. The basis of composition: layouts, cards and modals.
A value computed during render from props and state, such as a filtered list or a total, instead of stored in state, so it cannot get out of sync.
A development-only React wrapper that renders components twice and re-runs effects once extra, to expose impure rendering and missing cleanup.
A build-time plugin that adds memoization automatically, so manual useMemo, useCallback and memo are needed much less.
Components that run only on the server and send their result to the client, to reduce the JavaScript sent to the browser. Used in frameworks such as Next.js.
An async function used in a transition or a form action, with pending and error state tracked by React. Works with useActionState, useFormStatus and useOptimistic.
Hook that runs code after render to synchronise a component with the outside world. A dependency array decides when it re-runs, and a returned cleanup undoes it.
The second argument of useEffect, useMemo and useCallback. React re-runs them only when a listed value changed (Object.is). Include everything they read.
The function an effect returns. React runs it before the effect runs again and on unmount: unsubscribe, clear timers, abort requests.
Like useEffect but runs after the DOM update and before the paint. For measuring layout without a flicker. Blocks painting.
React 19.2 hook for a function that an effect can call and that always sees the latest props and state without being a dependency.
Two values are equal only if they are the same object in memory. A new object, array or function each render looks changed to memo and to dependency arrays.
Hook that caches a computed value until its dependencies change. For expensive calculations and stable object references.
Hook that keeps the same function instance between renders while its dependencies are unchanged. Useful for memo children and effect dependencies.
Wraps a component so it skips re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal to the last render.
Hook for state with many transitions. Components dispatch actions and a pure reducer returns the next state. dispatch is stable.
Passes a value to all descendants without props through every level. Every consumer re-renders when the provider value changes. Not a state manager.
Passing a prop through many intermediate components that do not use it, only to reach a deep child. Fixed with composition, context or a store.
A function named use... that calls other hooks to share stateful logic. Shares logic, not state: each call has its own state.
Hook that marks a state update as non-urgent so typing and clicks stay responsive while a heavy re-render runs in the background.
React component that shows a fallback while children wait for lazy-loaded code or data. Enables code splitting and streaming.
A component that catches errors thrown while rendering its children and shows a fallback. Does not catch errors in event handlers or async code.
Hook for subscribing to an external store, such as Redux or a browser API, safely with concurrent rendering.
Library for server data in React: caching by key, de-duplicated requests, retries, refetching and loading and error state. Replaces hand-written fetch effects.
Loading parts of an application on demand with dynamic import and React.lazy, so the first download is smaller.
Predictable state container: one store holds the app state, state changes only by dispatching actions, and pure reducers compute the next state.
The official, recommended way to write Redux: configureStore, createSlice (with Immer), createAsyncThunk, createEntityAdapter, createSelector and RTK Query.
The single object that holds the whole Redux state, runs the reducer on each dispatched action and notifies subscribers.
A plain object describing an event, by convention { type: "cart/itemAdded", payload }. Reducers respond to it. Name it as an event, not a setter.
A pure function (state, action) => nextState. It must not mutate state or cause side effects, because Redux detects change by reference.
Redux Toolkit function that defines a slice of state with its reducers and generates the action creators. Reducers may "mutate" because of Immer.
Library inside Redux Toolkit that gives reducers a draft they may mutate and produces a new immutable state, sharing unchanged parts.
Code between dispatch and the reducer that sees every action: logging, async thunks, analytics, listeners.
A function dispatched instead of an action so it can run async code and dispatch actions later. Handled by the thunk middleware.
A function (state) => value that reads from the store. useSelector re-renders the component when the result changes by reference.
Library behind createSelector: memoises derived data and recomputes only when its input selectors return different values.
Storing entities in an object keyed by id plus a list of ids, like database tables, so each entity has one copy and lookups are O(1).
Redux Toolkit middleware that runs side effects when matching actions are dispatched, as a lighter alternative to redux-saga.
Data-fetching and caching layer in Redux Toolkit. createApi generates hooks that cache by endpoint and arguments, share requests and refetch on tag invalidation.
RTK Query label: queries provide tags and mutations invalidate them, so affected queries refetch automatically.
Browser extension that shows every dispatched action and the state after it, with time-travel debugging.
React DevTools tab (and a component) that records renders: which components rendered, why, and how long each took. Use it on a production build before optimising.
Rendering only the rows visible in the viewport plus a few extra, so a list of 50,000 items keeps about 20 DOM nodes. Libraries: TanStack Virtual, react-window.
Google metrics for user-perceived performance: LCP (main content appears), INP (input to next paint) and CLS (layout shift).
Many fast unit tests, fewer component or integration tests, and a few end-to-end tests. Confidence per cost is highest in the middle for UI code.
Testing library that renders components in a real DOM and queries them like a user (by role, label, text). Tests behaviour, not implementation.
Fast test runner for Vite projects with a Jest-compatible API and native ESM. Jest is the long-standing alternative.
A browser-like DOM implemented in Node.js, used by Vitest and Jest so component tests run without a real browser.
Testing Library companion that simulates real user interaction (focus, typing, click) and is preferred over fireEvent. Its methods are async.
Library that intercepts network requests and returns fake responses, so components run their real fetch code in tests, Storybook and development.
Testing Library helper that runs a custom hook inside a test component so you can read its result and call its functions with act.
End-to-end testing tool that drives real browsers with auto-waiting, parallel runs and trace recording. Cypress is the common alternative.
A test that compares rendered output with a stored copy. Large snapshots are brittle and rarely catch real bugs, so prefer small explicit assertions.
A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change, usually from fixed sleeps, shared data or timing. Fix or remove it.
JavaScript runtime outside the browser: the V8 engine, libuv for the event loop and I/O, and core modules such as fs, http and stream. One main thread, non-blocking I/O.
Google JavaScript engine used by Chrome and Node.js. Compiles JavaScript to machine code with a just-in-time compiler and manages the heap and garbage collection.
Node.js class with on, once, off and emit, the Observer pattern behind streams, servers and sockets. Listeners run synchronously. An error event with no listener throws.
Object that handles data in chunks: Readable, Writable, Duplex or Transform. Keeps memory flat for big data and applies backpressure. Connect with stream.pipeline.
Node.js fixed-size block of raw bytes outside the JavaScript heap, used for files, sockets and encodings such as base64. A subclass of Uint8Array.
Node.js function that runs a callback in the check phase, right after the poll phase. Inside an I/O callback it always runs before setTimeout 0.
Node.js module that runs JavaScript on extra threads, each with its own event loop and heap, communicating by messages. For CPU-heavy work. Use a pool such as piscina.
Node.js module where a primary process forks workers that share one server port, to use all CPU cores. In containers, one process per container is more common.
Node.js module to start another OS process (spawn, fork, execFile). Prefer execFile with an argument array over exec to avoid command injection.
Signal asking a process to stop gracefully. A server handles it by closing listeners, finishing requests and exiting. SIGKILL cannot be caught.
Attack that sets __proto__ or constructor.prototype through unvalidated merged JSON, changing every object in the process. Validate input and avoid deep merges of untrusted data.
Regular expression denial of service: a pattern with nested quantifiers takes exponential time on crafted input and blocks the event loop.
The default Node.js package manager and registry. Uses package.json and a lockfile. pnpm and Yarn are alternatives; pnpm shares one store and is strict about dependencies.
Fast structured JSON logger for Node.js. Log objects with a request id instead of console.log strings.
HTTP connection reuse across requests. A shared agent with keep-alive avoids a new TCP and TLS handshake per call.
Delay between when a timer should fire and when it does. Rising lag means the main thread is blocked, the best health signal for a Node.js service.
Minimal web framework for Node.js: routing and a middleware chain on top of the http module. No ORM or validation included. Express 5 forwards async errors automatically.
A function (req, res, next) in the request pipeline. It can change req or res, end the response, or call next(). Runs in registration order. Four arguments make it an error handler.
Mini application that groups routes and middleware for one feature, mounted under a path prefix with app.use.
OPTIONS request a browser sends before a non-simple cross-origin call (JSON body, Authorization header, PUT or DELETE) to ask whether the origin, method and headers are allowed.
Express middleware that sets security-related HTTP headers such as Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options and Content-Security-Policy.
Capping requests per client in a time window, answered with 429 and Retry-After. Use a shared Redis store when running several instances.
Library that sends HTTP requests to an Express app in memory, without opening a port, so tests assert on status, headers and body.
Strategy-based authentication middleware for Express, wrapping login methods such as local, OAuth and JWT.
Vulnerability where a client sets fields it should not (role, balance) because the whole request body is copied into a model. Prevent it with strict schemas and field whitelists.
Fast Node.js web framework with a plugin system and built-in JSON-schema validation and serialisation. An alternative to Express.
Opinionated Node.js framework with modules, decorators and dependency injection, similar to Spring Boot. Runs on Express or Fastify.
Express setting that makes req.ip and req.protocol use forwarded headers from a load balancer or reverse proxy. Needed for correct rate limiting and secure cookies.
A set of reusable database connections created once per process, so requests do not open a new connection each time. Close it on shutdown.
A web app that loads one HTML page and JavaScript, then updates the screen and calls an API without full page reloads. The built files are static and served from a CDN.
One repository holding several projects (web app, API, shared packages) that are versioned and built together. With pnpm it uses workspaces.
The agreed shape of requests, responses and errors between front end and back end. Kept in one place: a shared zod package, an OpenAPI spec, or tRPC types.
Standard description of an HTTP API (paths, schemas, errors) in YAML or JSON. Used to generate servers, typed clients and documentation, and to detect breaking changes.
TypeScript library that lets a client call server functions with types inferred end to end, with no schema file. Fits a TypeScript monorepo.
Query language and typed schema where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs from one endpoint. An alternative to REST for many clients with different data needs.
Response header that lists the sources a page may load scripts, styles and connections from. A strong second defence against cross-site scripting.
Cookie holding a session id. Set httpOnly, Secure and SameSite so JavaScript cannot read it and cross-site requests do not carry it. Needs CSRF protection.
One-way stream from server to browser over plain HTTP with automatic reconnect. Simple choice for notifications and live feeds. WebSocket is the two-way alternative.
Lightweight PostgreSQL connection pooler. Many API instances connect to it so the database does not run out of connections. RDS Proxy is the AWS equivalent.
React framework that renders on the server, with routing, API routes and caching. Better first paint and SEO than a pure SPA, at the cost of a server to run.
Fast build tool and dev server for front-end projects. Serves modules in development, builds hashed static files for production, and can proxy /api to a local back end.
File that maps minified production JavaScript back to the original source so error trackers such as Sentry show readable stack traces.
W3C header that carries a trace id and span id between services, so one request can be followed from the browser through the API to the database.
